items.text: Accessible functors respect the cardinal filtration
$F\colon E\to E'$ accessible $\iff$ $F(E_\pi)\subset E'_\pi$ for some $\pi$ and $F$ is $\pi$-accessible.
Open: why $F(E_\pi)\subset E'_\pi$ for $\pi$ large. (SGA 4 argument escapes me.)
c=2^\pi\ \gg 0:\qquad F(E_c)\subset E'_c
F=\operatorname{Ind}_\pi(f_\pi),\qquad f_\pi\colon E_\pi\to E'_\pi
F(E_\pi)\subset E'_{\pi^{\pi_0}}\ \text{(SGA)};\qquad \pi=2^\lambda\ \Rightarrow\ \pi^{\pi_0}=\pi
If it holds for one $\pi$, it holds for all larger $\pi'$:
x=\varinjlim x_i,\ x_i\in E_\pi,\ |I|\le\pi',\ I\ \pi\text{-dominating}\ \Rightarrow\ F(x)=\varinjlim F(x_i)\in E'_{\pi'}
So any accessible functor respects the canonical filtration $(E_\pi)$, for $\pi$ large.
Other descriptions of accessibility
$C\subset E$ small subcategory, $i\colon C\hookrightarrow E$. Restriction functor:
i^*\colon \operatorname{Hom}(E,E')\to\operatorname{Hom}(C,E'),\qquad i_!\dashv i^*\ \ (\text{direct limits exist in }E')
$F$ accessible $\iff$ $F$ lies in the image of $i_!$ for some small $C$; the $i_!$ are fully faithful.
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{acc}}(E,E')=\bigcup_{C}\ i_!\operatorname{Hom}(C,E')
Limits in $\operatorname{Ind}_\pi(C)$
E=\operatorname{Ind}_\pi(C)\ \text{has arbitrary direct limits}\iff C\ \text{has direct limits indexed by categories of cardinality}\le\pi
Cut a direct limit in two: small pieces ($\le\pi$) and $\pi$-dominating index sets.
x_i\in C\ (i\in I):\quad \varinjlim_{I'\subset I}\Big(\varinjlim_{i\in I'}x_i\Big),\qquad |\mathrm{Ar}\,I'|\le\pi
Taken in $\operatorname{Ind}_\pi(C)$; checking uses: $\pi$-dominating direct limits commute with inverse limits of cardinality $\le\pi$.
The envelope $\operatorname{Ind}_\pi(C)$
$\Delta$: categories with arbitrary direct limits, functors commuting with them. $\Delta_\pi$: direct limits of cardinality $\le\pi$.
C\in\Delta_\pi \text{ small}:\qquad C\to\operatorname{Ind}_\pi(C)\ \ (\Delta_\pi\text{--}\Delta\ \text{envelope})
\operatorname{Hom}_{\varinjlim}\big(\operatorname{Ind}_\pi(C),F\big)\simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{\le\pi}(C,F)
Dually, with inverse limits: the envelopes of small objects of $\Delta_\pi$ are exactly the $\pi$-accessible categories.
Envelope of some $\Delta_\pi$, $\pi$ large $=$ accessible categories.
Categories coming from algebraic theories: stepwise, small data at each step, so come from some $\Delta_\pi$.
The category $S$ of set-realizations is $\operatorname{Ind}_\pi(C)$: accessible. $R=S^\circ$ is co-accessible.
\text{algebraic theories}\ \longleftrightarrow\ R\ \text{co-accessible}\ \longleftrightarrow\ S=R^\circ\ \text{accessible}
Representability and adjoints
Let $E$ be accessible and $F\colon E^\circ\to\mathbf{Sets}$ contravariant.
F\ \text{representable}\iff F\ \text{transforms direct limits of } E \text{ into inverse limits of Sets}
True for any $E$ with arbitrary limits and a small generating subcategory (SGA 4, 1.8); no accessibility needed.
Covariant $F\colon E\to\mathbf{Sets}$:
F\ \text{representable}\iff F\ \text{commutes with arbitrary inverse limits and } F\ \text{is accessible}
F\ \text{pro-representable (small index)}\iff F\ \text{left exact and accessible}\qquad(\text{SGA 4, I 8.13})
Representable $=$ pro-representable $+$ commutes with arbitrary inverse limits.
Left exact: a pro-object, maybe too large; accessible: small cardinality.
Adjoints
F\ \text{has a right adjoint}\iff F\ \text{commutes with arbitrary direct limits}
F\ \text{has a left adjoint}\iff F\ \text{commutes with inverse limits and is accessible}
Counterexample (SGA)
Groups: all simple groups, of arbitrarily high cardinality; their finite products form an inverse system.
The functor pro-represented by it has small values (simple subgroups of a given group have bounded cardinality) and commutes with inverse limits, but is not accessible.
Morphisms of algebraic theories
$T\leftrightarrow R$ (co-accessible) or $S$ (accessible); $S=T(\mathbf{Sets})$, $R=S^\circ$.
T\to T'\ \longleftrightarrow\ R'\to R\ \text{(commutes with inverse limits)}\ \longleftrightarrow\ S'\to S\ \text{(commutes with direct limits)}
u_*\colon S\to S',\ \ T(\mathbf{Sets})\to T'(\mathbf{Sets}):\quad\text{right adjoint of the functor } S'\to S
E.g. a functor transforming groups into monoids: usual groups become usual monoids.
u_*\ \text{comes from a morphism of theories}\iff u_*\ \text{has a left adjoint}\iff u_*\ \text{commutes with inverse limits and is accessible}
Stability of accessibility (SGA)
Fibred category $F/I$ over a small $I$; fibres $F_i$ accessible, transition functors $F_i\to F_j$ accessible.
\varprojlim_{2}F_i=\text{cartesian sections of } F/I\ \ \text{accessible};\ \text{also all sections}
Special case: constant system $F_i=E$.
E\ \text{accessible}\Rightarrow\operatorname{Hom}(I,E)\ \text{accessible};\quad \operatorname{Hom}(\widetilde I,E)\subset\operatorname{Hom}(I,E)
$\widetilde I$: the groupoid envelope of $I$.
Idea of proof: $\pi$ large, $F_i=\operatorname{Ind}_\pi(F_{i,\pi})$, transitions come from small functors.
\text{sections of } F_\pi/I \text{ form a small strictly generating subcategory}
Expected: $\pi$-accessible objects of $\varprojlim F_i$ $=$ sections of $F_\pi/I$ ($\pi$-accessible in the fibres).
The proof in SGA (about twenty pages) is messy; should be cleaned up.
2-direct limits
Is a 2-direct limit of accessible categories $E_i$ accessible? (functors commuting with direct limits)
Question only, no statement: the sum of two such categories (disjoint sum) has no direct limits.
Accessibility without direct limits: right notion unclear.
Recapitulation: algebraic theories

A theory is algebraic if built stepwise from a small set of base objects: at each step a small set of arrows, or small set of axioms (arrows invertible, pairs of arrows equal), or conjunction of a small set of structures.
Transfinite construction allowed.
T\ \longleftrightarrow\ R \ (\text{carries the universal structure});\quad T\to T'\ \longleftrightarrow\ R'\to R
$\Delta$-algebraic: $R$ co-accessible; $S=R^\circ$ accessible.
Non-algebraic theories
$R$ with a small strictly co-generating subcategory: every object of $S$ is a direct limit of objects of it.
F\colon R\to\mathbf{Sets}\ \text{commuting with inverse limits is representable;}\quad T(\mathbf{Sets})\simeq S
The theory is determined by its set-realizations, even if not algebraic.
u\colon R'\to R,\qquad u_C\colon T(C)\to T'(C);\qquad u_{\mathbf{Sets}}\colon S\to S'\ \ \text{(left adjoint)}
$S$ depends covariantly on $T$ — unlike $R$.
\operatorname{Hom}(T,T')\simeq\{S\to S'\ \text{with right adjoint}\}
Example: functor $\mathbf{Gp}\to\mathbf{Sets}$ commuting with inverse limits yet not accessible: not a morphism of theories.
A morphism of theories: monoid $\mapsto$ enveloping group; its adjoint goes with free structures.
Free structure: $S'=\mathbf{Sets}$, the underlying set functor and its left adjoint.
Fully faithful: subtheories
$S\hookrightarrow S'$ fully faithful with adjoint: a localisation functor.
Subtheories of $T'$: add axioms only, no new arrows.

\text{sub-theories of } T'\ \longleftrightarrow\ \Sigma'\subset\mathrm{Ar}(R')\ \text{stable under inverse limits}\ \longleftrightarrow\ \text{full subcategories of } S' \text{ stable under inverse limits}
Algebraic: $\Sigma'$ generated by a small set of arrows.
Is such a subcategory $S$ (stable under inverse limits, inclusion with adjoint) automatically accessible? Not clear; a counterexample?
